steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting an autoregressive diffusion model that generates raw speech waveforms directly. It should review two-stage, end-to-end, diffusion-based and large-scale speech synthesis approaches, motivate the autoregressive design, and state the contributions and paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Context: progress in speech technology and generative audio models
- Two-stage synthesis (decoder + vocoder) and its drawback
- End-to-end frameworks
- Diffusion models for speech
- Large-scale generative models and autoregressive generation
- Our model: DiffAR, related autoregressive diffusion work, contributions
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Context
  - last two decades: impressive progress in speech research and technologies
  - speech applications significant in communication, human-machine interaction
  - high-quality natural synthetic speech = text-to-speech (TTS)
  - research on deep-learning-based generative audio models: generation, enhancement, denoising, manipulation
- Two-stage synthesis
  - decoder + vocoder
  - decoder: reference signal (e.g. intended text) -> acoustic features via intermediate representations (mel-spectrograms); text-to-speech, image-to-speech, speech-to-speech
  - vocoder: acoustic features -> waveform
  - widely adopted; drawback: only magnitude (spectrogram), may neglect perceptual qualities from the phase
- End-to-end frameworks
  - single model, no explicit acoustic features
  - EATS, Wave-Tacotron, FastSpeech 2s: efficient end-to-end training, quality behind two-stage systems
  - VITS: normalizing flow + VAE + adversarial training -> high quality
  - YourTTS: VITS-like, zero-shot multi-speaker and multilingual
- Diffusion models for speech
  - strong in images, videos, speech
  - as decoders producing Mel-Spectrogram from text
  - DiffTTS: stochasticity -> one-to-many, same text spoken in diverse ways
  - Grad-TTS, ProDiff, PriorGrad, DiffGAN-TTS: faster synthesis, sometimes at cost of audio quality, stochasticity, simplicity
  - Guided-TTS: decoder, no transcript of target speaker, classifier guidance
  - DiffWave, WaveGrad, FastDiff: vocoders conditioned on Mel-spectrograms
  - DiffWave: also fixed-length vocabulary (ten digits), waveform directly, fixed 1 second -> no full sentences
  - WaveGrad 2: end-to-end; (i) Tacotron 2 encoder from phoneme sequence; (ii) decoder refining noisy waveform iteratively
- Large-scale models and AR generation
  - Voicebox (acoustic infilling), VALL-E (end-to-end, Codec representation): state of the art with extensive data; natural phenomena, in-context learning; robust to noise, generalize with thousands hours of speech
  - hard to replicate on smaller datasets
  - AR approach: long waveforms, sequential sample generation; slow inference
  - non-AR models: struggle with extremely long audio / long text, limited GPU memory
- DiffAR
  - autoregressive diffusion, raw waveforms, short overlapping frames
  - unconditional (no text) or conditional (text + linguistic parameters)
  - arbitrary duration unlike DiffWave; coherent temporal dependencies
  - end-to-end on raw waveform, no Mel-spectrogram; amplitude + phase -> human-like voice incl. vocal fry (irregular glottal opening, low pitch; American English: phrase finality, sociolinguistic factors, affect)
  - prior AR diffusion: video synthesis; ordered structures + efficiency; ours: one-dimensional time-sequential data, unlimited-duration speech
  - contributions (i) AR denoising diffusion for speech; (ii) unlimited durations, preserved computational resources; (iii) human-like voice incl. vocal fry, quality and variability vs state of the art
- Organization: Section 2 problem + AR diffusion; Section 3 text conditioning; Section 4 architecture; Section 5 results, comparison, ablation; Section 6 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Over the last two decades there has been impressive progress in speech-based research and technologies. Because of these advancements, speech applications became very significant in communication and in human-machine interactions. One part of this is generating synthetic speech that is high-quality and sounds natural, which is text-to-speech (TTS). In recent years a lot of research has been done on designing a deep-learning-based generative audio model. Such a model, if it is effective, can be used for speech generation, enhancement, denoising, and manipulation of audio signals.

Many neural generative models split the synthesis process into two separate components, a decoder and a vocoder. The decoder takes a reference signal, for example the text that should be synthesized, and turns it into acoustic features through intermediate representations like mel-spectrograms. What the decoder does exactly depends on the application, which can be text-to-speech, image-to-speech, or speech-to-speech. The vocoder then gets these acoustic features and generates the waveform that goes with them. This two-step approach is widely used, but one possible drawback is that it only focuses on the magnitude information (the spectrogram), and so it might neglect some natural and human perceptual qualities that can be derived from the phase.

End-to-end frameworks, by contrast, generate the waveform with a single model and do not explicitly produce acoustic features. EATS, Wave-Tacotron, and FastSpeech 2s were the models that pioneered efficient end-to-end training methods, but their synthesis quality is behind two-stage systems. VITS combines normalizing flow with VAE and adversarial training and gets high-quality speech. YourTTS uses an architecture similar to VITS and addresses zero-shot multi-speaker and multilingual tasks.

Recently diffusion models have shown impressive generative capabilities for synthesizing images, videos, and speech. For speech synthesis, many studies suggested using diffusion models as decoders that generate the Mel-Spectrogram representation from a given text. DiffTTS used the stochastic nature of diffusion models to capture a natural one-to-many relationship, so that the same text input can be spoken in different ways. Grad-TTS, ProDiff, PriorGrad, and DiffGAN-TTS tried to make the synthesis process faster. However this sometimes comes at the cost of audio quality, synthesis stochasticity, or model simplicity. Guided-TTS works as a decoder and does not need a transcript of the target speaker, it uses classifier guidance instead. DiffWave, WaveGrad and FastDiff on the other hand are vocoders, which generate waveforms by conditioning the diffusion process on the corresponding Mel-spectrograms. DiffWave can also learn the manifold of a limited, fixed-length vocabulary (the ten digits) and produce consistent word-level pronunciations. It works on the waveform directly but the speech it generates has a fixed duration of 1 second, so it cannot produce an entire sentence. Finally, WaveGrad 2 is an end-to-end model made of (i) Tacotron 2 as an encoder that extracts an abstract hidden representation from a given phoneme sequence; and (ii) a decoder that predicts the raw signal by refining the noisy waveform iteratively.

- Large-scale models and AR generation
  - Voicebox (acoustic infilling) and VALL-E (end-to-end, Codec representation): state of the art with extensive audio data, natural phenomena, in-context learning, robust to noise, generalize with thousands hours of speech
  - hard to replicate on smaller datasets
  - AR approach good for long waveforms (sequential samples at inference) but slow
  - non-AR models: extremely long audio / long text limited by GPU memory
- DiffAR
  - autoregressive diffusion model, raw waveforms, short overlapping frames
  - unconditional or conditional (text + linguistic parameters)
  - arbitrary duration (unlike DiffWave); coherent temporal dependencies
  - end-to-end on raw waveform, amplitude + phase -> human-like voice, vocal fry (definition)
  - prior AR diffusion work: video synthesis; ordered structures + efficiency; ours: one-dimensional time-sequential data
  - contributions (i)-(iii)
- Organization: Sections 2-6

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Over the last two decades there has been impressive progress in speech-based research and technologies. Because of these advancements, speech applications became very significant in communication and in human-machine interactions. One part of this is generating synthetic speech that is high-quality and sounds natural, which is text-to-speech (TTS). In recent years a lot of research has been done on designing a deep-learning-based generative audio model. Such a model, if it is effective, can be used for speech generation, enhancement, denoising, and manipulation of audio signals.

Many neural generative models split the synthesis process into two separate components, a decoder and a vocoder. The decoder takes a reference signal, for example the text that should be synthesized, and turns it into acoustic features through intermediate representations like mel-spectrograms. What the decoder does exactly depends on the application, which can be text-to-speech, image-to-speech, or speech-to-speech. The vocoder then gets these acoustic features and generates the waveform that goes with them. This two-step approach is widely used, but one possible drawback is that it only focuses on the magnitude information (the spectrogram), and so it might neglect some natural and human perceptual qualities that can be derived from the phase.

End-to-end frameworks, by contrast, generate the waveform with a single model and do not explicitly produce acoustic features. EATS, Wave-Tacotron, and FastSpeech 2s were the models that pioneered efficient end-to-end training methods, but their synthesis quality is behind two-stage systems. VITS combines normalizing flow with VAE and adversarial training and gets high-quality speech. YourTTS uses an architecture similar to VITS and addresses zero-shot multi-speaker and multilingual tasks.

Recently diffusion models have shown impressive generative capabilities for synthesizing images, videos, and speech. For speech synthesis, many studies suggested using diffusion models as decoders that generate the Mel-Spectrogram representation from a given text. DiffTTS used the stochastic nature of diffusion models to capture a natural one-to-many relationship, so that the same text input can be spoken in different ways. Grad-TTS, ProDiff, PriorGrad, and DiffGAN-TTS tried to make the synthesis process faster. However this sometimes comes at the cost of audio quality, synthesis stochasticity, or model simplicity. Guided-TTS works as a decoder and does not need a transcript of the target speaker, it uses classifier guidance instead. DiffWave, WaveGrad and FastDiff on the other hand are vocoders, which generate waveforms by conditioning the diffusion process on the corresponding Mel-spectrograms. DiffWave can also learn the manifold of a limited, fixed-length vocabulary (the ten digits) and produce consistent word-level pronunciations. It works on the waveform directly but the speech it generates has a fixed duration of 1 second, so it cannot produce an entire sentence. Finally, WaveGrad 2 is an end-to-end model made of (i) Tacotron 2 as an encoder that extracts an abstract hidden representation from a given phoneme sequence; and (ii) a decoder that predicts the raw signal by refining the noisy waveform iteratively.

Large-scale generative models like Voicebox and VALL-E get state-of-the-art results by using extensive audio datasets. Voicebox is an acoustic infilling model and VALL-E is an end-to-end model that uses Codec representation, and both are very good at simulating natural phenomena and they enable in-context learning. When they are trained on thousands hours of speech these models are robust to noise and can generalize. But it is a significant challenge to replicate this success on smaller datasets.

In parallel, long waveforms can be generated effectively with an autoregressive (AR) approach, where the waveform samples are generated one after the other in the inference phase. Autoregressive models work well for TTS, but inference is slow because they are sequential. On the other hand, non-autoregressive models have a hard time generating extremely long audio clips that correspond to a long text sequence, because GPU memory is limited.

In this work we propose a new autoregressive diffusion model that generates raw audio waveforms by producing short overlapping frames sequentially. We call our model DiffAR – Denoising Diffusion Autoregressive Model. It can work in an unconditional mode, where no text is given, or in a conditional mode, where text and other linguistic parameters are the input. Since the model is autoregressive, it can generate signals of any duration, unlike DiffWave. This lets the model keep coherent temporal dependencies and maintain critical characteristics. DiffAR is an end-to-end model that works directly on the raw waveform without any intermediate representation like the Mel-spectrogram. Because it considers both the amplitude and the phase components, it can generate a reliable, human-like voice that has everyday speech phenomena, including vocal fry. Vocal fry refers to a voice quality characterized by irregular glottal opening and low pitch, and it is often used in American English to mark phrase finality, sociolinguistic factors and affect.

We are not the first to introduce autoregressive diffusion models. One prior work proposed a method for video synthesis, and another one extended diffusion models to handle ordered structures while trying to make the process more efficient. Our model focuses on one-dimensional time-sequential data, especially high-quality speech generation of unlimited duration.

The contributions of the paper are: (i) an autoregressive denoising diffusion model for high-quality speech synthesis; (ii) the model can generate waveforms of unlimited duration while preserving the computational resources; and (iii) the model generates a human-like voice, including vocal fry, with high speech quality and variability compared to other state-of-the-art models.

The paper is organized like this. Section 2 formulates the problem and presents our autoregressive approach to the diffusion process for speech synthesis. DiffAR can be conditioned on input text, which is described in Section 3. Section 4 gives the details of the architecture of DiffAR. In Section 5 we present the empirical results, with a comparison to other methods and an ablation study. Section 6 concludes the paper.

steps.text:
In the last two decades, impressive progress has been made in speech-based research and technologies. With these advancements, speech applications have become highly significant in communication and human-machine interactions. One aspect of this is generating high-quality, natural-sounding synthetic speech, namely text-to-speech (TTS). In recent years, substantial research has been done to design a deep-learning-based generative audio model. Such an effective model can be used for speech generation, enhancement, denoising, and manipulation of audio signals.

Many neural-based generative models split the synthesis process into two distinct components: a decoder and a vocoder [1]. The decoder takes a reference signal, like the intended text for synthetic production, and transforms it into acoustic features using intermediate representations, such as mel-spectrograms. The specific function of the decoder varies based on the application, which can be text-to-speech, image-to-speech, or speech-to-speech. The vocoder, on the other hand, receives these acoustic features and generates the associated waveform [2]. Although this two-step approach is widely adopted [3,4,5,6], one potential drawback is that focusing only on the magnitude information (the spectrogram) might neglect certain natural and human perceptual qualities that can be derived from the phase [7].

By contrast, end-to-end frameworks generate the waveform using a single model without explicitly producing acoustic features. The models EATS [8], Wave-Tacotron [9], and FastSpeech 2s [3] pioneered efficient end-to-end training methods, but their synthesis quality lags behind two-stage systems. VITS [10] combines normalizing flow [11] with VAE [12] and adversarial training, achieving high-quality speech. YourTTS [13] adopts an architecture similar to VITS and addresses zero-shot multi-speaker and multilingual tasks.

Recently, diffusion models have demonstrated impressive generative capabilities in synthesizing images, videos, and speech. In speech synthesis, numerous studies have suggested using diffusion models as decoders to generate the Mel-Spectrogram representation from a given text. DiffTTS [14] used the stochastic nature of diffusion models to capture a natural one-to-many relationship, allowing a given text input to be spoken in diverse ways. Grad-TTS [15], ProDiff [16], PriorGrad [17], and DiffGAN-TTS [18] aimed to accelerate the synthesis process, which sometimes comes at the cost of audio quality, synthesis stochasticity, or model simplicity. Guided-TTS [19], functioning as a decoder, does not require a transcript of the target speaker and uses classifier guidance instead. In contrast, DiffWave [20], WaveGrad [4] and FastDiff [21] are vocoders that generate waveforms by conditioning the diffusion process on the corresponding Mel-spectrograms. DiffWave [20] can also learn the manifold of a limited, fixed-length vocabulary (the ten digits), producing consistent word-level pronunciations. It operates on the waveform directly but generates speech with a fixed duration of 1 second, so it cannot produce an entire sentence. Last, WaveGrad 2 [22] is an end-to-end model consisting of (i) Tacotron 2 [23] as an encoder for extracting an abstract hidden representation from a given phoneme sequence; and (ii) a decoder, which predicts the raw signal by iteratively refining the noisy waveform.

Large-scale generative models, such as Voicebox [24] and VALL-E [25], achieve state-of-the-art results by leveraging extensive audio datasets. Voicebox, an acoustic infilling model, and VALL-E, an end-to-end model utilizing Codec representation [26], excel in simulating natural phenomena and enable in-context learning. These models are robust to noise and able to generalize when trained on thousands hours of speech. However, replicating this success on smaller datasets is a significant challenge.

Parallel to that, long waveforms can be generated effectively using an autoregressive (AR) approach, which involves the sequential generation of waveform samples during the inference phase [27,25]. While autoregressive models work well for TTS, their inference is slow due to their sequential nature. On the other hand, non-autoregressive models such as [3,22] struggle to generate extremely long audio clips that correspond to a long text sequence due to the limited GPU memory.

This work proposes a novel autoregressive diffusion model for generating raw audio waveforms by sequentially producing short overlapping frames. Our model is called DiffAR – Denoising Diffusion Autoregressive Model. It can operate in an unconditional mode, where no text is provided, or in a conditional mode, where text and other linguistic parameters are used as input. Because our model is autoregressive, it can generate signals of an arbitrary duration, unlike DiffWave. This allows the model to preserve coherent temporal dependencies and maintain critical characteristics. DiffAR is an end-to-end model that works directly on the raw waveform without any intermediate representation such as the Mel-spectrogram. By considering both the amplitude and phase components, it can generate a reliable and human-like voice that contains everyday speech phenomena including vocal fry, a voice quality characterized by irregular glottal opening and low pitch, often used in American English to mark phrase finality, sociolinguistic factors and affect.

We are not the first to introduce autoregressive diffusion models. [28] proposed a method for video synthesis, and [29] extended diffusion models to handle ordered structures while aiming to improve efficiency in the process. Our model focuses on one-dimensional time-sequential data, particularly high-quality speech generation of unlimited duration.

The contributions of the paper are as follows: (i) an autoregressive denoising diffusion model for high-quality speech synthesis; (ii) the model can generate unlimited waveform durations while preserving the computational resources; and (iii) the model generates a human-like voice, including vocal fry, with high speech quality and variability compared to other state-of-the-art models.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formulate the problem and present our autoregressive approach to the diffusion process for speech synthesis. DiffAR can be conditioned on input text, as described in Section 3. Section 4 details the architecture of DiffAR. Next, in Section 5, we present the empirical results, including a comparison to other methods and an ablation study. We conclude the paper in Section 6.
